Graph-Anchored Knowledge Indexing for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a dominant paradigm for mitigating hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) by incorporating external knowledge. Nevertheless, effectively integrating and interpreting key evidence scattered across noisy documents remains a critical challenge for existing RAG systems. In this paper, we propose GraphAnchor, a novel Graph-Anchored Knowledge Indexing approach that reconceptualizes graph structures from static knowledge representations into active, evolving knowledge indices. GraphAnchor incrementally updates a graph during iterative retrieval to anchor salient entities and relations, yielding a structured index that guides the LLM in evaluating knowledge sufficiency and formulating subsequent subqueries. The final answer is generated by jointly leveraging all retrieved documents and the final evolved graph. Experiments on four multi-hop question answering benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of GraphAnchor, and reveal that GraphAnchor modulates the LLM’s attention to more effectively associate key information distributed in retrieved documents. All code and data are available at https://github.com/NEUIR/GraphAnchor .
1 Introduction

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Lewis et al. (2020) has emerged as a promising paradigm for mitigating hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) Brown et al. (2020) . For a given query, typical RAG models retrieve relevant documents, which are incorporated as contextual evidence to guide LLMs in generating accurate answers Ram et al. (2023) ; Shi et al. (2023) ; Li et al. (2024b) . Although RAG models have demonstrated effectiveness across many knowledge-intensive tasks Asai et al. (2024) , the retrieved contexts often contain substantial noise Wu et al. (2025b) , and supporting evidence is frequently distributed across multiple documents Li et al. (2024c) . The dispersed nature of key information across retrieved documents poses a challenge for RAG models in effectively integrating and leveraging the retrieved knowledge Kuratov et al. (2024) .

To address this issue, numerous studies have explored structuring retrieved knowledge to better aggregate supporting evidence distributed across multiple passages Li et al. (2024c) ; Li et al. (2025b) . These approaches typically investigate the effectiveness of different representation formats for extracting and representing salient information from retrieved evidence Wu et al. (2025a) ; Li et al. (2024c) ; Yu et al. (2025) . Although these methods enhance the coherence of knowledge representations and help reduce noise in the retrieved contexts, they primarily leverage these structures to filter out irrelevant information and assist LLMs in better utilizing the retrieved knowledge. As a result, they often fail to fully exploit crucial evidence that cannot be captured in these formats and overlook the role of structured data in facilitating deeper interpretation and reasoning over the retrieved knowledge Pankin (2013) . As shown in Figure 1 , graphs provide a well-defined structural representation for explicitly modeling entities and their relations. Such graphs can be incrementally updated by introducing newly identified entities, for example, adding “Carbon County” and linking it with “Red Lodge” through the “county seat” relation. This graph updating process progressively interprets the retrieved documents, which motivates us to treat the graph as a knowledge index for RAG systems.

This paper presents GraphAnchor, a Graph-Anchored Knowledge Indexing approach that iteratively updates a graph to enhance the interpretation of retrieved knowledge during the iterative retrieval process. Unlike previous methods Wu et al. (2025a) ; Li et al. (2024c) ; Yu et al. (2025) , GraphAnchor redefines the role of the graph, shifting it from a mere knowledge representation to an active indexing tool. At each retrieval step, GraphAnchor first retrieves documents based on the current query and updates the graph based on these retrieved documents. Then GraphAnchor assesses whether the current knowledge, informed by the graph, is sufficient to answer the query. If the knowledge is lacking, a new query is generated. Once the available knowledge is sufficient, the final response is generated according to the documents retrieved at each step with the final version of the graph.

Our experiments on four multi-hop QA datasets with different backbone LLMs demonstrate the effectiveness of GraphAnchor. Rather than refining knowledge for question answering, GraphAnchor focuses on knowledge anchoring and improves both the retrieval and QA modules within an iterative RAG framework. Specifically, GraphAnchor facilitates the retrieval of more relevant and diverse documents across multiple retrieval steps, and enables LLMs to better interpret and utilize the retrieved knowledge. Further analysis shows that, as the retrieval process progresses, the graph anchors an increasing number of related entities and relations into the index, and subsequently modulates the attention mechanism of LLMs to aggregate distributed evidence from the retrieved documents.
2 Related Work

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models typically retrieve relevant passages and incorporate them as contextual inputs, thereby helping Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate accurate and grounded responses Ram et al. (2023) ; Lewis et al. (2020) ; Shi et al. (2023) ; Shuster et al. (2021) . However, conventional RAG approaches often suffer from insufficient knowledge acquisition, particularly in multi-hop question answering scenarios where reasoning requires the integration of evidence across multiple passages.

To mitigate this limitation, several studies have proposed iterative retrieval strategies that progressively seek and accumulate relevant knowledge to support answer generation ( Trivedi et al., 2023 ; Jin et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . In addition, some methods perform deep retrieval by interacting with external retrieval tools during the reasoning process, enabling more flexible and adaptive information seeking Jin et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2025a) . Nevertheless, as the number of retrieval steps increases, these RAG systems inevitably introduce more noisy or irrelevant information, which can substantially degrade the quality of the generated outputs Cuconasu et al. (2024) .

To improve knowledge utilization in LLMs, prior work has explored reranking retrieved passages Asai et al. (2024) or summarizing salient information to filter out noise Vig et al. (2021) ; Wu et al. (2025b) . However, these approaches typically process retrieved passages in isolation, with limited modeling of relationships among different documents. As a result, cross-document evidence may be overlooked or insufficiently captured, particularly in settings that require aggregating complementary information across multiple sources Li et al. (2024c) . To better aggregate diverse knowledge from multiple retrieved passages, a growing body of work leverages structured representations, including schemas, tables, and graphs, to explicitly extract key information scattered across these retrieved documents Edge et al. (2024) ; Li et al. (2025b) ; Li et al. (2024c) ; Fang et al. (2024) ; Yu et al. (2025) . Liu et al. (2025) further explores multiple reasoning paths over the constructed knowledge graph, identifying conflicting paths as input context, thereby alleviating knowledge conflicts between internal and external information.

Instead of replacing retrieved passages with structured representations, some works Li et al. (2024a) ; Wang et al. (2024) construct graphs to identify related information across multiple passages or chunks. Specifically, they extract key entities and facts from different chunks or passages and connect them via a graph structure. Such graphs enable LLMs to better capture long-range dependencies and multi-hop relationships within long texts or across documents, thereby facilitating more effective localization of relevant evidence. In contrast, GraphAnchor maintains an evolved graph through iterative retrieval, which anchors key concepts for knowledge interpretation and subquery generation.
3 Methodology

As illustrated in Figure 2 , this section presents the proposed GraphAnchor, which introduces an evolving graph to anchor knowledge within an iterative RAG framework. We first describe the overall architecture of GraphAnchor, highlighting how the evolving graph is integrated to support reasoning, query generation, and question answering (Sec. 3.1 ). We then elaborate on the construction and dynamic updating of the graph, which functions as a context-aware knowledge index to enhance the knowledge association and comprehension capabilities of LLMs (Sec. 3.2 ).

3.2 Stepwise Graph Evolution for Context-Aware Knowledge Indexing

4 Experimental Methodology
In this section, we describe the datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details in our experiments. More experimental details are shown in Appendix A.2 .

Datasets. Following previous work Shao et al. (2023) , we use four multi-hop question answering datasets to evaluate the effectiveness of our method, including MuSiQue Trivedi et al. (2022) , HotpotQA Yang et al. (2018) , 2WikiMultihopQA (2WikiMQA) Ho et al. (2020) , and Bamboogle Press et al. (2022) .

Baselines. In our experiments, we compare GraphAnchor with the Vanilla RAG model Ram et al. (2023) and four multiple iterations retrieval models, including IRCoT Trivedi et al. (2023) , Iter-RetGen Shao et al. (2023) , DeepNote Wang et al. (2025) , and Search-R1 Jin et al. (2025) . For the vanilla RAG model, we follow previous work Ram et al. (2023) and feed 5 retrieved documents as context to answer the question. IRCoT and Search-R1 perform reasoning on retrieved knowledge and guide the model to retrieve missing information, so that accumulate more information. Iter-RetGen views the LLMs’ response generation on retrieved knowledge as needed information to retrieve new information. DeepNote dynamically refines the retrieved knowledge into a note for knowledge accumulation.

Evaluation Metrics. Following Wang et al. (2025) , we utilize Token-Level F1 (F1) and Exact Match (EM) as evaluation metrics. F1 score captures the trade-off between content coverage and redundancy, allowing for partial matches between the predicted and reference answers. Exact Match (EM) focuses on whether the model’s output exactly and completely matches the reference answer, providing a stricter measure of precision.

Implementation Details. We implemented GraphAnchor using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct Yang et al. (2024) , Qwen3-32B Yang et al. (2025) , and Llama3.1-8B-Instruct Dubey et al. (2024) as the backbone models. During retrieval, bge-large-en-v1.5 Xiao et al. (2024) is used to retrieve query-related documents, and the top 5 retrieved documents are fed into the LLM at each retrieval step. The maximum number of retrieval steps was limited to 4. All instruction templates used in GraphAnchor are shown in Appendix A.2 .
5 Evaluation Result

In this section, we first evaluate the performance of various iterative RAG reasoning methods, followed by an ablation study to investigate the contribution of individual modules in GraphAnchor. We then examine the role of the graph structure during the iterative process and analyze the effectiveness of GraphAnchor in knowledge anchoring and utilization. In addition, we evaluate Vanilla RAG under different retrieval depths in Appendix A.3 and analyze knowledge utilization across indexing formats in Appendix A.4 . We further report inference time for iterative RAG models in Appendix A.5 , along with attention visualizations cases in Appendix A.6 and a case study in Appendix A.7 .
5.1 Overall Performance
As shown in Table 1 , we report the performance of GraphAnchor along with several representative RAG baseline models.

The evaluation results demonstrate the effectiveness of GraphAnchor, which achieves more than a 3% improvement over all baseline models. Notably, these gains consistently generalize across different testing scenarios and backbone model scales, indicating strong robustness and generalization ability of GraphAnchor. Compared with deep retrieval-based methods such as IRCoT, Iter-RetGen, and Search-R1, GraphAnchor achieves approximately 10% improvements. This highlights the critical role of the constructed graph in facilitating effective understanding and utilization of retrieved knowledge across multiple retrieval iterations. Benefiting from the graph evolution process, GraphAnchor is able to interpret retrieved knowledge Pankin (2013) and provides a mechanism for anchoring essential information, thereby mitigating the negative impact of noisy retrieval results. Among all baseline models, DeepNote also improves the RAG performance during iterative retrieval by maintaining an explicit note to answer the given question, aiming to filter and refine retrieved knowledge before incorporation. In contrast, GraphAnchor shifts the focus from knowledge refinement to graph-based knowledge indexing through an evolving structure, which leads to more substantial performance gains on these QA tasks. It is worth noting that the graph constructed by GraphAnchor is designed to fully exploit the retrieved knowledge rather than replacing raw evidence with a new representation, thus avoiding the loss of potentially critical clues contained in the original retrieved documents.
5.2 Ablation Study
To better understand the contribution of each core component in GraphAnchor, we conduct ablation studies as shown in Table 2 .

Five ablation variants are compared. First, we evaluate GraphAnchor (QA w/ Docs) and GraphAnchor (QA w/ Graph) to assess the knowledge representation capability by prompting LLMs to answer questions based solely on retrieved documents and the constructed graph, respectively. Then, we implement GraphAnchor w/ Text Index, where the summarization results are used as the index for GraphAnchor, aiming to examine the effectiveness of structural representations for knowledge indexing. The instruction is shown in Appendix A.2 . Finally, we conduct GraphAnchor w/o Graph and GraphAnchor w/o Iterative Retrieval to analyze the roles of different model components.

When question answering relies only on the constructed graph (GraphAnchor (QA w/ Graph)), the RAG performance drops by approximately 3%. This indicates that the graph alone does not provide more effective knowledge for directly answering queries; instead, it serves as a form of knowledge anchoring that helps LLMs better interpret the retrieved information. Notably, for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, GraphAnchor (QA w/ Graph) performs worse than GraphAnchor (QA w/ Docs), suggesting that some necessary information may be lost during graph construction and evolution. Compared with GraphAnchor w/ Text Index, GraphAnchor achieves improvements of over 2%, demonstrating that structural representations, such as graphs, are beneficial for knowledge interaction and understanding during the indexing process.

We further analyze the effects of removing the iterative retrieval and graph modules. The evaluation results show that GraphAnchor w/o Iterative Retrieval suffers a performance drop of more than 10%, underscoring the critical role of iterative retrieval in incorporating sufficient knowledge for multi-hop QA tasks. When the graph is removed from both retrieval and QA stages of GraphAnchor, rather than only from the QA stage (GraphAnchor (QA w/ Docs)), the RAG performance decreases more substantially, by over 6% (about 2% more than the drop observed in GraphAnchor (QA w/ Docs)). This result indicates that the graph structure further facilitates iterative retrieval by enabling the generation of more effective subqueries, which in turn retrieve more relevant knowledge.
5.3 Effectiveness of Graphs in GraphAnchor During Iterative Retrieval

This subsection analyzes the effectiveness of the graphs constructed by GraphAnchor in the iterative retrieval process. We conduct experiments on the full HotpotQA dataset using the Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model to show the role of the graph in knowledge anchoring and retrieval.

Graph Effectiveness in Knowledge Anchoring. As shown in Figure 3 , we illustrate the knowledge anchoring effectiveness of the constructed graph at each retrieval step by analysing graph evolution and reporting the performance of RAG models as additional retrieved documents are incorporated.

First, Figure 3(a) presents the graph changes across different retrieval steps. Specifically, as the iterations proceed, the number of entities and triples steadily increases, indicating that the graph incrementally extracts key information from retrieved documents for indexing purposes. Notably, this growth continues to improve after the third retrieval step, while the hit rate of the ground-truth answer reaches a plateau. This observation suggests that the indexing process does not merely incorporate query-related entities and triples, but instead dynamically adjusts the graph structure to enable more effective knowledge indexing. Then, we evaluate the RAG performance at different retrieval steps using the F1 score in Figure 3(b) . Compared with the GraphAnchor (QA w/ Docs) model, GraphAnchor consistently outperforms it after the second retrieval step. This observation indicates that the benefits of the constructed graph are amplified with a deeper retrieval step, enabling effective utilization of accumulated knowledge.

Retrieval Effectiveness with Graph . Subsequently, we compute the document hit rate and the document set overlap rate to further analyse the role of the graph in knowledge retrieval. The performance of both GraphAnchor and GraphAnchor w/o Graph is shown in Figure 4 . As shown in Figure 4(a) , both methods benefit from iterative retrieval and exhibit steadily increasing document hit rates. Notably, GraphAnchor achieves consistently higher document hit rates by treating the graph as a dynamic index, which helps the model focus more on salient entities across multiple retrieval steps and thus facilitates more effective knowledge retrieval. In Figure 4(b) , GraphAnchor demonstrates a lower document overlap rate than GraphAnchor w/o Graph, which evaluates duplicate rate in all retrieved documents. This observation indicates that the graph functions as an effective dynamic indexing mechanism, reducing redundant documents during iterative retrieval.
5.4 Attention Visualization by Incorporating Knowledge Anchoring

In this subsection, we explore how the constructed graph assists LLMs in anchoring knowledge through the attention mechanism. We analyze the attention distribution when incorporating the constructed graphs for knowledge indexing. Instances from HotpotQA that require the maximum number of retrieval steps (4 steps) are selected to illustrate the knowledge anchoring mechanism.

Attention Distribution with Graph Anchoring. As shown in Figure 5 , we aggregate all retrieved documents as context and visualize the attention distribution on document tokens with graphs constructed at different retrieval steps.

First, we show the attention proportions of both retrieved documents and the graph during answer generation in Figure 5(a) to examine the role of the constructed graph. The results indicate that the graph typically receives the majority of attention from the LLM during question answering, and that attention weights increase as the graph is updated through more retrieval iterations. This demonstrates that the graph plays a crucial role in helping LLMs better answer queries, confirming its effectiveness in interpreting retrieved knowledge. Furthermore, Figure 5(b) presents the attention entropy when using the graph and the answer output as “queries” to document tokens. The results show that the attention entropy increases when graphs constructed at deeper iteration steps are used. This indicates that graphs built with more retrieval iterations enable LLMs to allocate attention more selectively to the more query-relevant document tokens, thereby highlighting the effectiveness of the graph in anchoring more distributed evidence from retrieved documents.
Knowledge Indexing via Graph Anchoring. Figure 6 illustrates the indexing mechanism, which computes attention weights over anchored entities mentioned in the retrieved documents.

In Figure 6(a) , we present the attention distribution over these graph-indexed entities mentioned in the retrieved documents across all retrieval steps. The index-related attention consistently increases as we utilize the graph constructed through successive retrieval iterations, indicating that the evolving graph progressively anchors key information from the retrieved documents at each step, forming part of the graph-based index maintained by GraphAnchor. Meanwhile, the perplexity of ground-truth answer generation steadily decreases, suggesting that the evolving graph index indeed helps LLMs leverage the retrieved documents more effectively for question answering. As shown in Figure 6(b) , we further examine the attention weights of the graph-anchored entities that are newly extracted from documents at different retrieval steps. The peak intensity along the diagonal indicates that, at each retrieval step, the newly graph-anchored entities receive substantially higher attention once the graph constructed at the corresponding retrieval iteration is incorporated. This observation suggests that the graph functions as a step-by-step indexing intermediate, effectively modulating the attention distribution of LLMs to facilitate more accurate knowledge interpretation and utilization.
6 Conclusion

This paper introduces GraphAnchor, a novel graph-based knowledge anchoring approach that reformulates the graph structure from a refined knowledge representation into an evolutive index for RAG. By dynamically updating the graph at each retrieval step, the proposed graph enables LLMs to anchor a broader set of related entities for knowledge utilization, which offers a new perspective for alleviating knowledge conflicts in LLMs.
Limitations

Although GraphAnchor demonstrates effectiveness in knowledge indexing for RAG systems, the quality of the constructed graph index remains constrained by the capabilities of the underlying LLM. Specifically, the performance of the proposed graph construction and utilization depends on the model’s ability to accurately extract, structure, and organize relevant information from retrieved documents. In addition, the current implementation represents the graph solely through verbalized entities and relations; more expressive and structured graph representation methods may further enhance performance.
